paras: The threatened lynching of Tom Manns, Ed Morris and Charles Sanders was a series of mob gatherings in Maysville, Kentucky, from February to June 1903 against three Black men accused of robbing and shooting John B. Farrow, an elderly farmer. On June 16, 1903, the three were tried under the guard of state troops with a Gatling gun and a Hotchkiss gun. No lynching took place; all three went to the penitentiary, and wire reports of the military guard ran across the country.

According to the Maysville Daily Public Ledger, three masked men entered Farrow's home near Mt. Gilead on the night of February 1, 1903, took $5 and shot him twice. Within two days police held Morris, Manns and Sanders, and a grand jury indicted them for burglary and shooting with intent to kill.

On February 3, the Louisville Courier-Journal reported, officers hurried the prisoners to the Covington jail "to avoid a mob that was coming to-night from Mt. Carmel, Mt. Gilead and Orangeburg." Several hundred men followed them to the depot and were held back with pistols, and an Orangeburg farmer, Charles G. Calvert, was arrested for trying to stop the removal.

On the night of June 3 a crowd the Bourbon News put at 300 to 500 waited at the Maysville depot for the prisoners while others guarded the approaches to the jail. The paper wrote that "a determined organization is ready to lynch the prisoners if they are brought back to Maysville." At Circuit Judge James P. Harbeson's request, Governor Beckham ordered about one hundred state troops to the town, and Harbeson refused a change of venue.

The troops brought the prisoners from Covington with Sheriff J. R. Roberson on the morning of June 16. According to a wire dispatch, farmers filled the town, and when "shouts from the leaders of the mob" rose during the march from the jail, the troops fixed bayonets and held the crowd in a square while the prisoners were taken to court. The Wheeling Register's dispatch put the crowd at more than 5,000 and said it would have lynched the men but for the militia.

On June 18 Sanders testified that Manns was the "leading spirit" in the affair, pleaded guilty and received five years, the legal limit. Manns was convicted of shooting Farrow with intent to kill and Morris pleaded guilty, and each also received five years. The next day Morris and Mann received ten more years each for burglary, and troops escorted the prisoners to Frankfort. Apart from Calvert's arrest, no report of charges against members of the crowds appears in the coverage.

The local Ledger regretted the "warlike demonstration" and urged citizens to avoid violence. Yet its editorial said the troops were "not here simply to protect three worthless Negroes" but "to prevent a repetition of the scene of some three years ago." After the verdicts it headlined "THREE CAPITAL PRIZES!" and declared that "the mob spirit has been suppressed."

Elsewhere the story ran as wire copy, with the Salt Lake Herald's "LYNCHING FEARED" saying troops were sent "to prevent a repetition of the Coleman affair." The Walla Walla Evening Statesman headlined its dispatch "Three Negro Rapists on Trial" and called the charge murder, and the Seattle Star reprinted it as "MILITARY PREVENTS LYNCHING." A Richmond report added that the prosecutor might have the men pardoned and retried for murder if Farrow died, "so that they can be executed."

In the Black press, the St. Louis Palladium ran the wire report as "TROOPS GUARD AT TRIAL," with a subhead calling Sanders a "Negro Murderer" given "a Light Sentence," and added no comment. The State Ledger printed a short, belated Frankfort item about the troops.

Most reports gave the charge as robbery and shooting with intent to kill, but one wire version called it murder and its headline called the men rapists. The local trial reports support the first version, since Farrow was alive and a murder trial was possible only if he died within a year.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Tom Manns, Ed Morris and Charles Sanders
bases: Crowds gathered three times to seize and lynch three jailed Black men, but troops and officers kept them off and no one was attacked (A3, A5, A11, A17).
The local Ledger, the Courier-Journal, the Bourbon News and independent wire dispatches agree that crowds gathered to lynch the prisoners and that troops guarded the trial (A3, A5, A10, A11, A17).

framing.detail: The local Ledger opposed mob violence but called the accused 'three worthless Negroes' and headlined the verdicts 'THREE CAPITAL PRIZES!'.
Distant papers ran wire dispatches headlined 'LYNCHING FEARED', 'MILITARY PREVENTS LYNCHING' and 'Troops Avert Lynching', with one headline calling the men 'Rapists'.
The St. Louis Palladium ran the wire under 'TROOPS GUARD AT TRIAL' with the subhead calling Sanders a 'Negro Murderer' who received 'a Light Sentence'; the State Ledger ran a short Frankfort item.

versions.value: Robbery and shooting with intent to kill; Farrow alive

conflicts.note: The local Ledger's trial reports are better evidence: the men were convicted of shooting with intent to kill and could be tried for murder only if Farrow died within a year.
Different dates; the 5,000 figure appears only in the Wheeling dispatch.
Reports over time; none reports his death.
Same text; the Seattle Star dateline is evidently a misprint, since the trial opened Tuesday, June 16.
